name: Heightpill / height blackpill

chain: Height viewed as top dating factor
Motivation to gain height or compensate
angle.text: Looksmaxxing and incel-adjacent forums use the heightpill to describe the belief that height largely decides a man's dating outcomes, which drives interest in lifts, surgery and styling. Research shows a preference for taller partners on average, not an absolute rule.

summary: The belief that height decides a man's dating fate; research shows a taller-partner preference, not an iron rule.
note: Preferences are real in some studies but vary by culture and trade off against other traits.
currentQuick:
The heightpill is the belief that a man's height largely determines his dating and social success and that nothing else can fully make up for being short. It is a staple of looksmaxxing and blackpill forums.
Research reports that many women prefer taller men and that shorter men are rated less favourably on average, but people also trade height against income and education, and preferences differ across cultures.
How it works: It is a belief or framework rather than a practice. Believers treat height as a fixed trait; some respond with height-altering measures discussed in other entries.
Risks and caveats: The main documented concern in discussions is psychological distress among teens and men who fixate on height. Measures used to change height carry their own medical risks.
deepLead:
The heightpill (or height blackpill) is a belief, widespread on looksmaxxing and incel-adjacent forums, that a man's height is among the most decisive factors in dating and social outcomes, and that short stature cannot be offset by other traits. The term follows the "pill" vocabulary of online manosphere communities, where a "pill" is a supposedly uncomfortable truth.
Adherents commonly describe a threshold, often framed in feet and inches, below which they say a man is at a major disadvantage. Published research gives a more mixed picture: studies report that many women prefer taller male partners and that shorter men are rated less favourably on average, while other work finds that people trade height off against other traits and that preferences vary across cultures.

name: Mazdutide

angle.text: Fat-loss-focused users discuss mazdutide, a weekly injectable GLP-1 and glucagon dual agonist, as a route to lower body fat and a leaner look. It is approved in China for weight loss, and trials have measured weight change rather than appearance.

summary: Weekly GLP-1/glucagon dual agonist approved in China for weight loss; strong trial data, but regional approval only.
note: Approved only in China; investigational elsewhere. Trials mostly in Chinese adults.
currentQuick:
Mazdutide is a once-weekly injection that activates both GLP-1 and glucagon receptors, developed by Innovent and Eli Lilly. It was approved for weight management in China in June 2025.
A phase 3 placebo-controlled trial in Chinese adults with obesity or overweight reported meaningful weight loss. Participants in most trials have been Chinese adults.
How it works: The GLP-1 component reduces appetite and slows gastric emptying; the glucagon component is proposed to increase energy expenditure.
Risks and caveats: Trials describe GI side effects typical of GLP-1 drugs. It is a prescription drug in China and investigational elsewhere, so use outside approved markets means unregulated supply.
deepLead:
Mazdutide (also IBI362 and LY3305677) is a once-weekly injectable peptide that activates both the glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptor and the glucagon receptor. It was developed by Innovent Biologics together with Eli Lilly, and received marketing approval in China in June 2025.
In a phase 3 placebo-controlled trial in Chinese adults with obesity or overweight, once-weekly mazdutide was reported to produce clinically relevant weight loss versus placebo. Earlier trials and a meta-analysis reported weight loss in people with and without diabetes. It is a prescription drug in China and investigational elsewhere; it appears in looksmaxxing discussions as a possible next-generation fat-loss peptide.

name: Orforglipron

angle.text: Fat-loss-focused users discuss orforglipron, a once-daily GLP-1 pill that is not a peptide, as an oral alternative to injectables for getting leaner. Phase 3 trials have measured weight loss, and appearance outcomes have not been studied directly.

summary: Once-daily GLP-1 pill that isn't a peptide; phase 3 weight loss data and a US label, still newer than injectables.
note: Prescription-only with GLP-1-class warnings; boxed thyroid C-cell tumour warning.
currentQuick:
Orforglipron is a once-daily pill from Eli Lilly that activates the GLP-1 receptor without being a peptide, so it needs no injection. It is sold in the US as Foundayo for chronic weight management.
Phase 2 and 3 trials reported dose-related weight loss versus placebo over 72 weeks in adults with obesity.
How it works: It binds and activates the human GLP-1 receptor, which regulates appetite and food intake.
Risks and caveats: Common effects are gastrointestinal. The label warns about thyroid C-cell tumours, pancreatitis, kidney injury and other effects, and advises stopping in pregnancy.
deepLead:
Orforglipron (LY3502970), marketed as Foundayo, is a once-daily oral, non-peptide small-molecule agonist of the GLP-1 receptor developed by Eli Lilly for obesity and type 2 diabetes. Unlike injectable peptide drugs such as semaglutide, it is a small molecule taken by mouth.
A phase 2 trial and a phase 3 trial in adults with obesity reported dose-related weight loss versus placebo over 72 weeks. A US drug label states it is indicated, with diet and physical activity, to reduce excess body weight and maintain weight reduction in adults with obesity, or overweight with at least one weight-related condition, and carries a boxed warning about thyroid C-cell tumours that applies to the GLP-1 class. Grokipedia reports FDA approval on April 1, 2026.

name: Oral semaglutide (Rybelsus)

angle.text: Fat-loss-focused users discuss oral semaglutide as a tablet form of the GLP-1 drug used for getting leaner. It is proven for type 2 diabetes and a weight-loss version is approved; trials measure weight rather than appearance.

summary: Semaglutide as a daily tablet: proven for type 2 diabetes, with a weight-loss version now approved.
note: Boxed thyroid C-cell tumour warning; prescription-only.
currentQuick:
Oral semaglutide is the pill version of the GLP-1 drug semaglutide, sold as Rybelsus for type 2 diabetes. An oral version for weight management was approved in the US in December 2025 under the Wegovy name.
Absorption by mouth is low, so it is combined with an absorption enhancer.
How it works: It activates GLP-1 receptors, affecting appetite and blood sugar. The tablet formulation includes an enhancer that helps absorption in the stomach.
Risks and caveats: Common effects are nausea, diarrhoea, vomiting and constipation. The label carries a boxed thyroid C-cell tumour warning, and it is contraindicated with certain thyroid cancer histories.
deepLead:
Oral semaglutide, sold as Rybelsus, is a tablet form of the GLP-1 receptor agonist semaglutide. It was the first GLP-1 receptor agonist developed for oral administration, co-formulated with an absorption enhancer, sodium N-(8-[2-hydroxybenzoyl] amino) caprylate, that helps the peptide survive the stomach.
Rybelsus was approved in the US in September 2019 and in the EU in April 2020 for type 2 diabetes; in December 2025 the FDA approved an oral semaglutide for weight management under the Wegovy brand. Its use for weight loss in people without diabetes is discussed in appearance and fat-loss communities, where the pill is sometimes regarded as an alternative to injections.

name: Garcinia cambogia

angle.text: Users take garcinia cambogia, sold for its hydroxycitric acid, as a fat burner to get leaner. Human trials and reviews have measured body weight and mostly report small effects; appearance changes have not been studied.

summary: HCA-based fat-burner supplement; trials and reviews mostly find weak effects, with some liver-injury reports in blended products.
note: Liver toxicity has been reported with multi-ingredient products containing the extract.
currentQuick:
Garcinia cambogia is a tropical fruit whose rind contains hydroxycitric acid (HCA), sold as an over-the-counter weight-loss supplement.
A 1998 JAMA trial and later systematic reviews of weight-loss supplements describe limited or inconsistent evidence of benefit.
How it works: In the lab, HCA inhibits ATP-citrate lyase, an enzyme involved in making fatty acids, which is the basis for claims that it reduces fat storage.
Risks and caveats: Reported effects include nausea, stomach discomfort, headache and dry mouth. Liver toxicity has been reported with products containing the extract, and it may interact with some medicines.
deepLead:
Garcinia cambogia, now classified as Garcinia gummi-gutta, is a tropical fruit tree native to the Western Ghats of southwestern India. Its fruit rind is used as a sour flavouring in curries, and its principal acid, hydroxycitric acid (HCA), is extracted and sold as a weight-loss dietary supplement.
HCA inhibits the enzyme ATP-citrate lyase in laboratory work, which led to claims that it could lower fat synthesis. A 12-week randomised controlled trial in JAMA tested the extract for body weight and fat mass, and systematic reviews of weight-loss supplements have generally rated the evidence as weak. Cases of liver injury have been reported with multi-ingredient supplements that contained it.

name: Raspberry ketones

angle.text: Supplement users take raspberry ketones as a fat burner on the strength of cell and rodent findings. Human weight-loss trials are essentially absent, so the use rests mostly on marketing and anecdote.

summary: A raspberry-aroma compound sold as a fat burner; human weight-loss evidence is essentially absent and safety data are thin.
note: Sold as a supplement, but no regulator has approved it for weight loss and published human safety data are limited.
currentQuick:
Raspberry ketone is the main aroma molecule of red raspberries and is widely used as a flavouring and in perfumery. Supplements containing it, usually made synthetically, are marketed as fat burners.
Research on its weight-loss effect is mostly in rodents and cell cultures. Encyclopedic summaries state that no clinical evidence of weight loss in humans has been established.
How it works: Proponents say it boosts fat breakdown and raises adiponectin or norepinephrine signalling. Laboratory studies in obese rats have reported changes in lipid levels, insulin resistance and adipose-tissue gene expression, including the water-and-glycerol channel aquaporin 7. A small registered human study (NCT06681597) examined circulating FGF21 and energy expenditure, but its results are not described in the sources available.
Risks and caveats: The US FDA classed raspberry ketone as generally recognised as safe only as a food flavouring in tiny amounts. Safety of supplement-level intake in people is poorly characterised. Case reports describe coronary vasospasm and ventricular tachycardia in people taking raspberry ketone weight-loss products, and a 2015 toxicology paper and a Danish university warning raised concerns about supplement use.
deepLead:
Raspberry ketone (4-(4-hydroxyphenyl)butan-2-one, also called rheosmin or frambinone) is a phenolic compound that gives red raspberries much of their characteristic smell. It also occurs in cranberries and blackberries, and is used in perfumery, cosmetics and as a food flavouring. 
Because raspberries contain only a few milligrams per kilogram, commercial supplements generally rely on synthetically produced raspberry ketone.  Products are marketed for weight loss and fat burning, a use that grew from rodent studies on adipose tissue and lipid metabolism. 
Wikipedia states that there is no clinical evidence for a weight-loss effect in humans, and that no international regulatory authority has approved it as a weight-loss supplement.  Published case reports describe cardiac events in people taking such products, though a causal link has not been established.

name: Conjugated linoleic acid (CLA)

angle.text: Users take CLA, a fatty acid found in ruminant meat and dairy, to reduce body fat and get leaner. Mouse results were striking, while human trials have measured body composition and report small or short-lived changes.

summary: A fatty acid from ruminant fat sold as a body-fat reducer; mouse results were striking, but human trials show small or no lasting changes.
note: A 2012 meta-analysis found no long-term body-composition effect in overweight people, and a 2018 meta-analysis reported higher inflammatory markers.
currentQuick:
Conjugated linoleic acids are a family of fatty acids found mainly in meat and dairy from ruminants such as cattle and sheep. Supplements are sold for fat loss and as a bodybuilding aid.
The interest started with mouse experiments in the late 1990s that reported large drops in body fat. Human trials have generally shown much smaller effects, and Wikipedia cites a 2012 meta-analysis finding no long-term effect on body composition in overweight or obese people.
How it works: In rodents, the t10,c12 isomer was linked to body-composition changes and increased activity of carnitine palmitoyltransferase, an enzyme involved in moving fat into mitochondria for burning. The c9,t11 isomer is the main form in food and appears to have different biological effects. How well these mechanisms carry over to humans is unresolved.
Risks and caveats: Wikipedia cites a 2018 meta-analysis of randomised trials reporting that CLA supplementation may raise C-reactive protein and TNF-alpha. The US FDA categorised CLA as generally recognised as safe for use in foods in 2008. Supplement quality, isomer mix and long-term effects in humans remain areas of ongoing research.
deepLead:
Conjugated linoleic acid (CLA) refers to a group of positional and geometric isomers of linoleic acid whose double bonds are conjugated. The most abundant forms are cis-9,trans-11 (rumenic acid) and trans-10,cis-12. They occur naturally in the meat and dairy fat of ruminants, produced by rumen microbes. 
CLA became a weight-management supplement after a 1997 mouse study reported 57 to 60 percent lower body fat in animals fed a CLA-supplemented diet.  A later mouse study attributed the body-composition changes to the trans-10,cis-12 isomer. 
Human trials have been less dramatic. Wikipedia reports that a 2012 systematic review and meta-analysis found no long-term effect on body composition in overweight or obese people, and that a 2018 meta-analysis found CLA supplementation may increase inflammatory markers.

name: Forskolin

chain: Claimed fat breakdown and lean mass shift
angle.text: Users take forskolin, a Coleus forskohlii extract, as a fat burner to get leaner and sometimes to support body composition. The cAMP effect in cells is well documented; supplement claims rest on small human studies of lower quality.

summary: A Coleus plant compound that raises cAMP in cells and is sold as a fat burner; supplement claims rest on small, low-quality studies.
note: A standard lab tool for raising cAMP; Wikipedia describes the early weight-loss studies as low quality and inconclusive.
currentQuick:
Forskolin is a diterpene isolated from the roots of Coleus forskohlii (also called Coleus barbatus or Plectranthus barbatus), a plant used in Ayurvedic medicine. In laboratories it is a standard reagent for switching on the cell-signalling molecule cAMP.
Supplement makers market Coleus extract for fat loss and lean mass. Wikipedia describes the early human weight-loss studies as low quality with inconclusive results.
How it works: Forskolin directly activates adenylyl cyclase, the enzyme that makes cyclic AMP (cAMP). cAMP is a second messenger that acts through protein kinase A and EPAC. In fat cells, raised cAMP is associated with fat breakdown (lipolysis), which is the basis for the weight-loss claims.
Risks and caveats: Wikipedia gives only chemical hazard information and does not describe adverse effects in people. Because forskolin influences cAMP signalling in many tissues, including heart and blood vessels, laboratory work has studied cardiovascular effects. Human safety data for long-term supplement use are limited.
deepLead:
Forskolin, also called coleonol, is a labdane diterpene obtained from the roots of Coleus forskohlii, a plant in the mint family used in traditional Ayurvedic medicine.  It was identified in the 1970s and became a widely used biochemical tool because it activates adenylyl cyclase and raises intracellular cAMP. 
Dietary supplements containing Coleus extract are marketed for fat loss and body composition. Wikipedia characterises the early weight-loss research as low quality and inconclusive, and notes that newer laboratory work suggests bioavailability strongly affects any anti-obesity effect.  Grokipedia, an AI-generated source, states that some clinical studies reported modest fat-mass reductions. 
Other human research has focused on glaucoma and, in smaller studies, on supplementation with exercise.

name: Fucoxanthin

angle.text: Supplement users take fucoxanthin, a brown-seaweed pigment, as a fat burner based on rodent data. Human evidence is scant, and absorption of the compound appears low.

summary: A brown-seaweed pigment sold as a fat burner on the strength of rodent data; human evidence is scant and bioavailability appears low.
note: Anti-obesity findings come mainly from rodents; Wikipedia notes limited human studies indicate low bioavailability.
currentQuick:
Fucoxanthin is an orange-brown carotenoid pigment found in brown seaweeds such as wakame and in diatoms. It is sold in supplement form, often as seaweed or microalgae extract, for fat loss and metabolic health.
The fat-loss pitch grows out of rodent experiments, notably a 2005 study showing lower abdominal fat in rats and mice fed lipids from Undaria pinnatifida. Human data are limited to a few small trials.
How it works: In the rodent work, fucoxanthin was linked to expression of uncoupling protein 1 (UCP1) in white fat, a protein that normally makes heat in brown fat. Laboratory studies also report antioxidant and anti-inflammatory activity in cells. Whether these effects occur at supplement intakes in people is not established.
Risks and caveats: Reviews report fucoxanthin to be well tolerated in animals, and seaweed has long been eaten as food. Human safety data for concentrated supplements are limited, and the compound is sensitive to light, heat and oxygen. Wikipedia lists a GHS eye-irritation hazard (H319) for the pure chemical.
deepLead:
Fucoxanthin is a xanthophyll carotenoid (C42H58O6) that serves as a light-harvesting accessory pigment in brown macroalgae and diatoms, and gives them their olive-brown colour. It was first isolated in 1914 by Willstatter and Page from brown algae. 
Interest in fucoxanthin as an appearance-related supplement began with rodent studies reporting less abdominal white fat and increased UCP1 expression after feeding lipids from the edible seaweed Undaria pinnatifida.  Reviews describe additional antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, antidiabetic and anticancer activity, mostly in cells and animals. 
Wikipedia notes that limited human studies indicate low bioavailability.  Grokipedia, an AI-generated source, states that large human trials are scarce.

name: Glucomannan

angle.text: Dieters take glucomannan, a konjac fibre that forms a gel in the stomach, to feel fuller and eat less while getting leaner. It is sold for appetite control; meta-analyses of weight loss report small changes.

summary: Konjac fibre that swells into a gel in the stomach; sold for appetite control, with meta-analyses finding little to no clinically meaningful weight loss.
note: Health Canada advises taking it with plenty of fluid and not at bedtime because of choking and blockage risks.
currentQuick:
Glucomannan is a soluble dietary fibre extracted mainly from the konjac corm; about 40 percent of its dry weight is glucomannan. It is used as a food thickener, in shirataki noodles and konjac jellies, and as a weight-loss supplement.
Wikipedia reports no good evidence that it causes weight loss as of 2020, citing a meta-analysis that found a non-significant difference of about 0.22 kg versus placebo. Since 2010 EU law has nonetheless allowed a weight-loss claim for overweight people on calorie-restricted diets, based on an EFSA opinion.
How it works: Glucomannan absorbs water and forms a viscous gel in the stomach, which proponents say increases fullness and slows nutrient absorption. A meta-analysis suggests it may lower LDL cholesterol by up to 10 percent, and a trial in type 2 diabetes reported effects on the appetite hormone ghrelin.
Risks and caveats: Taken with too little water, glucomannan products can cause choking or bowel obstruction. Common effects are diarrhoea, belching and bloating. The US FDA barred konjac jelly candies from import in 2001 over choking hazards, and the FTC has taken action against some supplement marketers over weight-loss claims.
deepLead:
Glucomannan is a water-soluble polysaccharide and dietary fibre made of beta-1,4-linked mannose and glucose units, found in the cell walls of several plants. The konjac corm is its main commercial source, at about 40 percent by dry weight. 
It is used as a thickener and emulsifier (E425(ii)), in shirataki noodles and konjac jelly snacks, and as a supplement marketed for weight loss, constipation and cholesterol reduction. The proposed mechanism is that the gel formed in the stomach promotes fullness. 
Wikipedia reports that, as of 2020, there was no good evidence that glucomannan causes weight loss, while a meta-analysis suggests it may lower LDL cholesterol by up to 10 percent.  Regulators differ: the EU has allowed a weight-loss claim since 2010 under defined conditions, while the US FTC has pursued supplement marketers over misleading claims.

name: Psyllium husk

angle.text: Users take psyllium fibre to feel fuller between meals, so it is easier to hold a calorie deficit and lean out for a more defined face and body. It is well studied for digestion and cholesterol, and trials on weight loss report small effects.

summary: Gel-forming soluble fibre from Plantago seed husks; well studied for constipation and cholesterol, with only minor weight-loss effects reported.
note: Needs adequate fluid to avoid choking or obstruction; 2024 testing found lead in all nine psyllium supplements tested.
currentQuick:
Psyllium is a viscous soluble fibre made from the seed coat of Plantago species, mainly Plantago ovata, grown largely in northern India. It is a long-standing over-the-counter fibre supplement and is used in baking and as a food thickener.
It is also marketed as a fullness aid for weight control. Wikipedia cites a 2023 review reporting only minor weight loss over 12 weeks in people with overweight or obesity, from low-to-moderate quality studies. Its better-supported effects are on constipation, LDL cholesterol and blood sugar.
How it works: Psyllium is not absorbed by the small intestine. It absorbs water to form a gel that softens stool and adds bulk. The fullness effect proposed by marketers is attributed to the same gel; the mechanisms behind its cholesterol and blood-sugar findings are not detailed in the sources reviewed.
Risks and caveats: Common effects are gas, bloating and abdominal pain. Taken with too little water it can thicken in the throat and cause choking or bowel obstruction. Allergic reactions including anaphylaxis occur, especially among people occupationally exposed to the powder. Wikipedia reports that ConsumerLab found lead in all nine psyllium supplements it tested in 2024.
deepLead:
Psyllium, also called ispaghula or isabgol, is obtained from seeds of Plantago species, chiefly Plantago ovata. The seed coat is milled into a white husk that absorbs water to form a gel; the gel-forming polysaccharide has been characterised chemically.  India produces most of the world supply. 
It is best known as a fibre supplement for constipation and, in the US, as the active ingredient in Metamucil, introduced by G.D. Searle in 1934 and later acquired by Procter & Gamble.  Trials and meta-analyses have also examined its effect on cholesterol and blood glucose. 
Psyllium is marketed for weight loss on the basis of fullness, but Wikipedia reports that a 2023 review found only minor weight loss over 12 weeks in overweight or obese people, based on low-to-moderate quality evidence.

name: Apple cider vinegar

angle.text: Apple cider vinegar is drunk diluted for fat loss and used as a skin toner and hair rinse for clearer skin and shinier hair. Small trials exist on weight, while the skin and hair uses rest on anecdote.

summary: Fermented apple juice drunk diluted for fat loss and clear skin; trials are small and major references describe no good evidence for weight loss.
note: Undiluted vinegar and tablets have been linked to tooth enamel and esophageal injury; may interact with insulin and diuretics.
currentQuick:
Apple cider vinegar is made by fermenting apple juice first into alcohol and then into acetic acid. It is a common kitchen ingredient and has a long folk-medicine history. In looksmaxxing forums it is promoted as a cheap all-round ingredient for fat loss, skin, hair and digestion.
Published reviews summarised by Wikipedia and Grokipedia describe limited or poor-quality evidence for weight loss. Small studies have looked at blood glucose and cholesterol with modest results, and the Mayo Clinic is quoted as saying it is unlikely to cause meaningful weight loss.
How it works: The active component is generally taken to be acetic acid, about 5 percent of the liquid. Proposed explanations for metabolic effects include slower stomach emptying and effects on post-meal glucose and insulin. Topical claims for acne and dandruff rest on its acidity and in-vitro antimicrobial activity. Which of these mechanisms matter in people has not been established.
Risks and caveats: Reported problems include tooth enamel erosion, throat or esophageal injury from tablets, reflux and stomach upset, and skin burns or eye injury when used undiluted on the body. Possible interactions with insulin and diuretics are noted. Food amounts are generally regarded as safe by regulators; supplements are not regulated as medicines for weight loss.
deepLead:
Apple cider vinegar (ACV) is a vinegar made from apple juice by two-step fermentation: yeast convert sugars to alcohol, then acetic acid bacteria convert the alcohol to acetic acid. The finished product is roughly 94 percent water and 5 percent acetic acid with almost no fat, protein or micronutrients. Unfiltered versions contain a cloudy cellulose-and-bacteria sediment called the mother. 
Besides cooking and preserving, ACV is promoted in wellness and looksmaxxing communities as a drink for fat loss and appetite control and as a skin toner, hair rinse and dandruff treatment. Wikipedia states that there is no high-quality clinical evidence that regular consumption helps with weight loss or maintenance, and that major health bodies do not recommend it for therapeutic use.  Grokipedia cites the Mayo Clinic as saying it is unlikely to cause meaningful weight loss and cites meta-analyses suggesting modest effects on blood glucose and cholesterol in some trials. 
Reported adverse effects include dental enamel damage, esophageal injury from tablets, and gastrointestinal discomfort.

name: Green coffee bean extract

angle.text: Users take green coffee bean extract as a fat-loss pill aimed at a leaner physique. It has been studied for blood pressure and metabolic markers, and its best-known weight-loss study was retracted, so the appearance claim is largely untested.

summary: Unroasted-coffee chlorogenic acid pill sold for fat loss; the best-known supporting study was retracted and the FTC acted against marketers.
note: Weight-loss marketing led to FTC settlements in 2014-2015; human trials are small and of poor quality per reviews.
currentQuick:
Green coffee bean extract is made from unroasted coffee beans, which are rich in chlorogenic acid. It is sold in capsule form as a fat-burning and appetite supplement.
A 2011 meta-analysis found tentative weight-loss effects but poor evidence quality, and a 2017 review concluded human studies were too poor to draw conclusions. A widely cited 2012 trial was retracted in 2014, and US regulators took action against several marketers.
How it works: Chlorogenic acid is proposed to slow carbohydrate absorption and change fat and glucose metabolism; animal studies in mice reported less fat accumulation on diets containing the extract. Human mechanisms have not been firmly established.
Risks and caveats: Trials in people with mild hypertension reported blood pressure effects with the extract and no major adverse events in small samples. Products contain varying amounts of chlorogenic acid and sometimes caffeine. The supplement is sold as a dietary supplement rather than a licensed drug.
deepLead:
Green coffee bean extract (GCE) is a concentrate of unroasted coffee beans, standardised in supplements to chlorogenic acid, a polyphenol that is largely lost in roasting.  It has been sold as a weight-loss supplement and studied for blood pressure and metabolic markers. 
Wikipedia states that clinical evidence is insufficient to show that it works or is safe for weight loss. A 2011 systematic review of randomised trials found tentative evidence of weight loss but of poor quality, and a 2017 review of chlorogenic acid concluded that human studies were of poor quality and no conclusions could be drawn. 
The extract was promoted on The Dr. Oz Show in 2012, and in 2014-2015 the US Federal Trade Commission took action against several marketers, including settlements with Applied Food Sciences, which had sponsored the main trial cited in advertising.

name: Chromium picolinate

chain: Lower body fat, more muscle definition
angle.text: Chromium picolinate is marketed to curb sugar cravings, cut fat and support muscle development. Reviews have looked at body weight and lean mass and report no reliable effects, so the link to a leaner look is a marketing belief.

summary: Chromium supplement sold to curb cravings and cut fat; reviews report no reliable evidence of weight or muscle effects.
note: Rare case reports of kidney and liver injury at high intakes; may interact with diabetes medicines.
currentQuick:
Chromium picolinate is a form of trivalent chromium bound to picolinic acid, sold as a supplement for weight loss, muscle building and blood sugar support. Forum interest centres on claims that it reduces carbohydrate cravings.
A 2013 Cochrane review, as summarised by Wikipedia, found no reliable evidence to draw firm conclusions on weight loss or muscle gain in overweight adults. The European Food Safety Authority found insufficient evidence for a body-weight effect.
How it works: Chromium is proposed to enhance insulin signalling, sometimes through a peptide called chromodulin. Wikipedia reports that the insulin-receptor effects were seen in vitro but not adequately shown in living organisms, and the exact mechanism is unknown.
Risks and caveats: Typical supplement amounts show little evidence of toxicity. Reported effects include allergic reactions, headache, insomnia and irritability, and rare case reports describe kidney or liver injury at high intakes. It may interact with insulin and other drugs. Regulators have approved only a heavily qualified US health claim about insulin resistance.
deepLead:
Chromium(III) picolinate is a pink-red coordination compound of trivalent chromium and picolinic acid, sold as a dietary supplement and marketed in the United States to athletes for muscle development and for weight loss. 
Whether chromium is an essential nutrient is debated; the European Food Safety Authority found no convincing evidence to justify intake recommendations.  Reviews of supplementation report either no effect on muscle or fat or a small weight loss in trials longer than 12 weeks, and a 2013 Cochrane review found no reliable evidence for firm conclusions.  A 2004 systematic review of dietary supplements for body-weight reduction also examined such products. 
In 2005 the US FDA allowed only a qualified health claim describing a relationship to insulin resistance and type 2 diabetes risk as highly uncertain.

name: Detox / slimming teas

angle.text: Users drink detox and slimming teas to de-bloat and drop scale weight quickly before events or photos. The change is typically fluid and gut contents rather than fat, and a 2015 review found no compelling evidence for detox claims.

summary: Herbal teas, often senna-based, sold to cleanse or slim; the weight change is typically fluid, and a 2015 review found no compelling evidence for detox claims.
note: Senna-containing teas act as stimulant laxatives; reported effects include cramps, diarrhea and potassium loss.
currentQuick:
Detox or slimming teas are herbal blends marketed for cleansing and weight loss. Many rely on senna, a plant whose sennosides are a stimulant laxative.
A 2015 review of detox diets, summarised by Wikipedia, found no compelling evidence for weight management or toxin elimination, and weight lost on such regimens is typically regained. Few trials of the teas themselves are listed.
How it works: Senna is thought to increase fluid and electrolytes in the large bowel and stimulate gut movement, so apparent weight change largely reflects stool and water loss rather than body fat.
Risks and caveats: Reported senna effects are abdominal cramps, diarrhea, nausea and flatulence, and lower potassium, which can increase digoxin toxicity. Regular use can cause melanosis coli, a brown discoloration of the colon wall. Senna is contraindicated in intestinal obstruction and some inflammatory bowel conditions.
deepLead:
Detox or slimming teas are herbal beverages sold to cleanse the body of toxins or aid weight loss; many contain senna, an anthraquinone plant laxative. 
Detox diets in general claim to remove toxins through restricted intake or purging. A 2015 review concluded there was no compelling evidence supporting detox diets for weight management or toxin elimination.  Senna glycosides are an established stimulant laxative used for constipation and bowel preparation.

name: Laxatives for weight loss

chain: Flatter-looking stomach for a short time
angle.text: Some people take laxatives to drop scale weight and look flatter. Reviews describe the loss as mostly water and classify the behaviour as purging linked to eating disorders, so it is documented as a weight-control practice rather than a fat-loss method.

summary: Using laxatives to drop scale weight; reviews say the loss is mostly water, and use is linked to later eating disorders and electrolyte harms.
note: Associated with later eating-disorder diagnosis and potentially fatal electrolyte disturbances. Help is available from eating-disorder services.
currentQuick:
Some people use over-the-counter laxatives to lower the number on the scale quickly. This is sometimes described as water-weight loss.
Published sources describe the weight change as mainly temporary fluid loss rather than calorie loss, and a large US cohort study linked laxative and diet pill use for weight control to later eating-disorder diagnosis in young women.
How it works: Laxatives act in the large intestine after nutrients have already been absorbed in the small intestine, so they mainly remove water and electrolytes rather than calories.
Risks and caveats: Reported harms include dehydration, low blood pressure, electrolyte and acid-base disturbances that can be potentially fatal, kidney damage, and colonic problems. Laxative misuse is tied to anorexia nervosa and bulimia nervosa in clinical literature.
deepLead:
Laxative use for weight control means taking laxatives not to treat constipation but to reduce body weight.  It is classified in clinical literature as a purging behaviour associated with eating disorders. 
Wikipedia notes that laxatives speed passage through the large intestine after nutrients are absorbed, so weight changes mainly reflect temporary fluid loss.  A prospective study of 10,058 US women followed from 2001 to 2016 examined diet pill and laxative use for weight control and subsequent first eating-disorder diagnosis.

name: Compounded semaglutide / microdosing GLP-1

chain: Lower body fat, leaner face and body
angle.text: Users take compounded or gray-market semaglutide, often at below-label amounts, to cut appetite and body fat for a leaner face and physique. Fat loss is established at approved doses in trials, while the microdosing version has not been studied.

summary: Pharmacy-made or gray-market semaglutide, often used at below-label amounts; the fat-loss drug is proven at approved doses, the microdosing version is not.
note: FDA does not review compounded drugs and has reported dosing-error adverse events.
currentQuick:
Compounded semaglutide is the same active ingredient as Ozempic or Wegovy, prepared by a compounding pharmacy rather than the manufacturer. Microdosing means using less than the label amount, a practice that appears in fat-loss and longevity circles.
Approved semaglutide has strong trial evidence for weight loss at labeled doses. For microdosed or compounded versions, evidence is limited to a narrative review and early-stage registered trials.
How it works: Semaglutide activates GLP-1 receptors, which raises glucose-dependent insulin release, lowers glucagon and acts on the hypothalamus to reduce appetite and slow gastric emptying.
Risks and caveats: Common effects are nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, abdominal pain and constipation. The FDA reports adverse events linked to dosing errors, off-label dosing, unapproved salt forms, improper shipping and counterfeit products, and does not evaluate compounded drugs for safety or effectiveness.
deepLead:
Compounded semaglutide is semaglutide, the active ingredient in the approved drugs Ozempic, Wegovy and Rybelsus, that a compounding pharmacy has prepared as a custom product rather than the manufacturer's branded pen or tablet. "Microdosing" GLP-1 refers to an informal practice in which people use amounts smaller than the doses on the approved label, often drawn from multi-dose vials, with the stated aims of reducing appetite and body fat with fewer side effects or lower cost.
In the United States the FDA listed Ozempic and Wegovy as being in shortage starting in August 2022, and federal law allows compounding pharmacies to prepare versions of drugs on the shortage list under certain conditions. The FDA does not review compounded drugs for safety or effectiveness, and it has published warnings about dosing errors, doses above the approved label, unapproved salt forms of semaglutide, counterfeit products and products sold "for research purposes."
Semaglutide at approved doses has been studied in large randomized trials for diabetes and obesity. Evidence about microdosed regimens is limited to a narrative review and registered trials that are early or not yet reporting; no published controlled trial has established the effects of low-dose compounded semaglutide on appearance or body composition.

name: Calorie deficit / calorie counting

angle.text: A calorie deficit tracked by counting is the baseline method in looksmaxxing circles for cutting body fat to reveal jawline, cheekbones and abs. Fat loss from a deficit is well established, while evidence specific to facial appearance is limited.

summary: Eating below maintenance and logging it: the standard way to lose fat, with limited evidence specific to facial appearance.
note: Severe restriction is associated with muscle loss and other effects.
currentQuick:
A calorie deficit means consuming less energy than you burn. Calorie counting is tracking intake to keep that gap, and it is the usual foundation of a cut in looksmaxxing circles.
Calorie restriction is well established to produce weight and fat loss, though the intake best for health is not known and there is little research on appearance outcomes specifically.
How it works: When intake is below energy expenditure, the body draws on stored energy, mostly fat but also some lean tissue.
Risks and caveats: Reported effects include cold sensitivity, hormonal and menstrual changes, and, in severe restriction as in the Minnesota experiment, muscle wasting, anemia and depression. Moderate restriction may be harmful for people who are already lean.
deepLead:
A calorie deficit means eating less energy than the body uses, and calorie counting is the practice of tracking food intake, usually with an app or scale, to maintain that gap. In looksmaxxing communities it is the baseline method for losing body fat to reveal facial and body definition, often called "cutting."
Calorie restriction, the research term, is defined as reducing energy intake below energy requirements without causing malnutrition. Wikipedia notes that it causes weight and fat loss, while the calorie intake and fat mass best for human health are not known. US dietary guidelines and scientific societies recommend calorie control for people with overweight.

name: High-protein diet

angle.text: Users eat protein-forward to hold onto muscle while dieting and to stay full on fewer calories, giving a leaner, more muscular look. The muscle and fullness benefits are supported in studies, while claims of better hair and skin are untested.

summary: Protein-forward eating for muscle retention and fullness; supported for those goals, untested for hair or skin claims.
note: Kidney effects at very high intakes are debated; people with kidney disease are advised to consult clinicians.
currentQuick:
A high-protein diet raises protein above the standard 0.8 g/kg recommended allowance, usually through meat, fish, eggs, dairy and legumes. It is popular for cutting and muscle building.
Higher intake is linked to more muscle and less muscle loss during energy deficits; claims about hair or skin have not been tested.
How it works: Protein increases satiety, has a higher thermic effect than carbohydrates or fat, and supplies amino acids for muscle repair.
Risks and caveats: Reviews disagree on kidney risk at higher intakes. Restrictive versions may cause constipation, headaches or bad breath, and the AHA has cautioned about diets high in saturated fat.
deepLead:
A high-protein diet emphasizes protein-rich foods such as meat, fish, eggs, dairy and legumes. Definitions vary: Wikipedia describes it as drawing 40 percent or more of daily calories from protein, while other sources use thresholds above the US recommended dietary allowance of 0.8 grams per kilogram of body weight per day, or around 1.2 to 2.0 g/kg for active people.
Within looksmaxxing communities, protein is discussed for building muscle, staying full while cutting, and supporting hair, skin and other tissues; a recent social-media trend called "protein maxxing" focuses on maximizing intake. Research links higher protein intake to greater muscle mass and less muscle loss during energy deficits, while reviews disagree on kidney and cardiovascular risks.

name: OMAD (one meal a day)

angle.text: Users eat all daily food in one sitting as a simple way to run a calorie deficit and lean out. It is a form of time-restricted eating, and no trials have tested OMAD specifically for appearance.

summary: All daily food in one sitting: an intermittent-fasting variant with no OMAD-specific trials behind it.
note: Not recommended for pregnancy, adolescents, or people with eating disorders.
currentQuick:
OMAD means eating one meal a day, usually in a one- to two-hour window. It is a form of intermittent fasting used by people trying to cut fat.
Broader intermittent fasting research shows modest weight loss, but no trials were found on OMAD specifically.
How it works: Compressing eating into one window tends to lower total daily intake, producing a calorie deficit.
Risks and caveats: Short-term hunger, irritability, dizziness and headaches are reported. Health bodies advise against intermittent fasting for pregnant women, children, older adults, underweight people and those with eating disorders.
deepLead:
OMAD stands for "one meal a day", an eating pattern in which all daily food is consumed in a single sitting, usually within a one- to two-hour window. Wikipedia classifies it as a subtype of time-restricted eating within intermittent fasting.
Looksmaxxing forum users discuss it as a way to cut body fat, sometimes alongside low-carbohydrate eating or fat-loss drugs. Reviews of intermittent fasting report modest weight loss, with limited evidence that it outperforms continuous calorie restriction, and no trials specific to OMAD and facial appearance were found.
